idiom_name: sorted effective-dated struct array with a hand-written lower-bound accessor
implementation_notes: C has no ordered container and no date type beyond time_t/struct tm, so the temporal collection is a struct holding an array of {effective date, value} milestones kept sorted by date, plus an accessor that returns the greatest milestone whose date is not after the requested one. bsearch(3) is the only standard primitive and it matches an exact key, not 'greatest key <= key', so the lookup is a hand-written lower-bound loop over the array (or a custom comparison wrapper around bsearch); qsort maintains the order when a version is added. What replaces the classic structure: nothing - the structure must be written, which makes the interval bookkeeping as reviewable (and as error-prone) as any other pointer code; the classic form stays the only option in C, so the value of the pattern here is the accessor pair and the fixed bound convention, not the container.
pitfalls: time_t is a point in time, not a calendar date: mktime() normalises out-of-range fields and applies the local zone/DST, so a 'date' stored via mktime can land on the previous or next day - store civil dates (yyyymmdd integers) or compare in UTC only.
lo - 1 on a size_t underflows when no milestone is in force (lo == 0); the guard must come before the decrement, which is exactly the class of bug a typed container would have prevented.

Returning a pointer into the milestone array ties the caller to the store's lifetime: any realloc when a version is appended invalidates it, so the accessor should copy the value or document the ownership window.

A put() that inserts into the middle of the array is an O(n) memmove plus a re-sort; without an explicit 'one version per date' rule, a repeated put at the same date silently replaces the stored value.
